11.01.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is this knee prosthesis?"
- "A **total knee**: femoral component, tibial tray, polyethylene (PE) insert, ± patellar button."
- "I name it by **constraint**: what it holds that the knee can no longer hold."

- More constraint → more stability, less motion, more loosening (Handbook)

| Implant | Look for | Holds |
|---|---|---|
| **Cruciate-retaining (CR)** | open notch, no box | PCL kept |
| **Posterior-stabilised (PS)** | femoral **box**, tibial **post** | cam–post replaces PCL |
| **Constrained condylar (CCK)** | deep box, tall wide post, stems | adds varus–valgus |
| **Rotating hinge** | axle links femur to tibia | everything, even hyperextension |
| **Unicompartmental (UKA)** | one condyle, one plateau | one compartment |
| **Patellofemoral (PFA)** | trochlear flange, button | patellofemoral only |

- By compartments: unicompartmental, bicompartmental, tricompartmental
- Modern systems share cuts: CR can be changed to PS, even CCK, in theatre

- Constraint ladder: CR, PS, PS beside high-post constrained
- PS total knee on AP, lateral and skyline views

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Keep it, substitute it, post it tall, hinge it**

11.02.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "name the parts of this knee"
- "Metal **femoral component**, metal **tibial tray** with a keel, PE **insert** locked on top."
- "A dome-shaped all-PE **patellar button** if the patella is resurfaced."

### The parts
- Femoral component: two condylar runners join in front as the **patellar flange**
- It is cobalt-chrome (CoCr); oxidised zirconium is a harder, scratch-resistant option

- Tibial tray: metal baseplate, keel or stem, and a locking mechanism
- Insert: ultra-high-molecular-weight PE, at least **8 mm** thick (Campbell)
- Patellar button: all-PE dome, cemented on the cut patella

- Retrieved PS knee: femur, tray, insert, button; post wear

### Highly cross-linked PE in the knee
- Less wear in simulators; but the PS post is under **shear**
- Some makers add **vitamin E** to the PE instead

- Gamma sterilisation in air → a subsurface **white band** in the PE (Campbell)
- Worst series: UKAs stored on the shelf 4.4 years or more
- **49%** of them failed at 18 months

### Modular tray vs all-PE tibia
| | Modular metal tray | All-PE tibia |
|---|---|---|
| Parts | baseplate + insert | one piece |
| Plus | insert exchange, stems, augments | cheap, no backside wear |
| Minus | **backside wear** under the insert | harder to cement |
| Best for | almost everyone | low-demand elderly |

- Backside wear = micromotion between tray and insert → osteolysis
- All-PE tibia bends at its rim → cement cracks → loosening

- Total condylar knee with a one-piece all-PE tibia

11.03.t: 11.3 CR vs PS — The Full Card
11.03.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "CR or PS — how do you tell?"
- "PS: a **box** between the femoral condyles and a **post** on the insert."
- "CR: open notch, flatter insert; the patient's own PCL does the rollback."

| (Handbook) | CR | PS |
|---|---|---|
| PCL | kept | removed |
| Femur | open notch | **box cut** |
| Insert | flatter | dished, central post |
| Rollback by | native PCL | cam strikes post |
| Balancing | harder | easier |

- **Rollback**: the femur's contact point moves back as the knee bends
- No rollback → the posterior femur hits the insert → flexion stops
- The cam meets the post at about **70°** of flexion (Campbell)
- The PS post stops the tibia sliding back; it gives no varus–valgus stability

- Normal rollback: contact point moves back with flexion
- Cam–post drives rollback; PS knee in deep flexion

### Recognise it
- PS femur: a box (housing) between the condyles, cam at its back
- Chamfer cuts for CR; extra box cut for PS

### CR — when, and its price
- Keeps bone, keeps proprioception, restores the joint line more easily
- Avoid CR in varus over **10°**
- Avoid CR in valgus over **15°**

- A tight PCL lifts the front of the insert in flexion → **lift-off**
- Lift-off rocks the tray like a see-saw: wear, then loosening (Prof Mahmoud Abdel Karim)
- Late PCL rupture → flexion instability → revision to PS

- Tight PCL lifting the trial insert; stepwise PCL release

### PS — when, and its price
- PS is a must in **inflammatory arthritis**, after **patellectomy**, and with PCL injury (Miller)
- Most Egyptian surgeons use PS: patients come late, balancing is easier (Prof Mostafa Shokry)
- The box removes notch bone → condylar fracture risk

- **Cam jump**: loose flexion gap → cam rides over the post; revise
- **Patellar clunk**: scar nodule above the patella catches in the box; excise it

- PS insert: front of the post worn by the box
- Patellar clunk: scar nodule catching in the femoral box

PITFALL — "which wears more, CR or PS?"
- Handbook: the flat CR insert wears more; Miller: CR slides forward → sliding wear
- PS adds its own wear at the post and cam
- Say → "**CR: sliding wear on a flat insert. PS: wear on the post.**"

11.04.t: 11.4 Other Inserts — Deep-Dish, Medial Pivot, Mobile Bearing
11.04.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is this insert with a high front lip?"
- "An **ultracongruent** (deep-dish, anterior-stabilised) insert on a CR femur: PCL removed, no box cut."

### Ultracongruent (anterior-stabilised)
- A raised anterior lip stops the femur sliding forward (Miller)
- A rescue in theatre when the PCL is lost or over-released
- Minimal rollback; a loose flexion gap → mid-flexion instability

- Deep-dish CR insert: built-up front lip

### Medial pivot
- Medial side is a **ball in socket**; lateral side is free to roll back

- Medial pivot cam design; medial pivot knee on X-ray

### Fixed vs mobile bearing
| | Fixed bearing | Mobile bearing |
|---|---|---|
| Insert | locked on tray | rotates on polished tray |
| Plus | simple, forgiving | low contact stress, self-aligns |
| Minus | rotation must be perfect | backside wear, **spin-out** |

- A mobile insert **follows the femur**, not the tibia
- Wrong tibial rotation: the insert ends ≈ **15°** turned on the tray (Prof Mostafa Shokry)
- The turned insert sticks out → arthrofibrosis

- Survival is the same as fixed bearing
- **Spin-out**: loose flexion gap → tibia rotates behind the femur (Miller)
- Reduce at 90° with the leg hanging; then revise the gap

- Retrieved rotating-platform knee: insert on polished tray
- Bearing spin-out: insert behind the lateral femoral condyle

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Lip in front, pivot inside, spin needs a loose gap**

11.05.t: 11.5 Constrained Implants — CCK and Rotating Hinge
11.05.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is this knee with stems and a tall post?"
- "A **constrained condylar knee**: a tall, wide post in a deep box gives varus–valgus stability."
- "If the collaterals and the posterior capsule are both gone → **rotating hinge**."

### CCK (varus–valgus constrained)
- A PS design whose larger post fits the box walls: little toggle
- It does **not** stop hyperextension → no use in recurvatum (Handbook)
- Stems in femur and tibia share the higher load

| CCK indication (Miller) | Why |
|---|---|
| Residual flexion-gap laxity | commonest reason |
| MCL or LCL attenuation | post replaces the ligament |
| Severe valgus with weak MCL | complex primary |
| Revision with instability | stems + augments needed |

- Primary CCK: **97.6%** survival at 10 years (Campbell)

- CCK: enlarged post in deepened box
- Unstable CR knee revised to a stemmed constrained knee

### Rotating hinge
- Femur and tibia are **linked**: hinge connector, connecting pin, tibial yoke
- The tibial yoke turns in a rotating platform → less torque on the bone
- A built-in extension stop → blocks recurvatum

| Hinge indication | Example |
|---|---|
| Global instability | MCL gone, gaps unbalanceable |
| **Hyperextension** (absolute) | polio, spina bifida |
| Massive bone loss | tumour, fracture, infection |
| Salvage revision | failed constrained knee |

- Keep hinges for these cases: more complications in primary TKA (Campbell)

- Rotating hinge parts: connector, pin, yoke, platform
- Rotating hinge implant
- Hinged knee after two failed TKAs: AP and lateral

PITFALL — "a PS knee for an MCL-deficient knee?"
- The PS post is not constrained: it resists sliding, not opening
- Say → "**No. Collateral lost → CCK; collateral and capsule lost, or recurvatum → rotating hinge.**"

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **One wall down → tall post; walls and back down → hinge**

11.06.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is this half-knee?"
- "A **medial UKA**: one femoral condyle and one tibial plateau resurfaced, cruciates kept."
- "**Oxford** = mobile bearing; flat PE on a metal tray = fixed bearing."

- UKA relies wholly on the native ligaments; medial UKA is by far the commonest
- Quicker recovery, less pain, better function than TKA (Miller)
- Long-term survival is lower than TKA

| UKA indications | UKA contraindications |
|---|---|
| Isolated medial arthritis | inflammatory arthritis |
| Pain in that compartment | arthritis in other compartments |
| **Intact ACL** | **ACL deficient** |
| Correctable deformity | fixed deformity over 5–10° |
| Flexion arc over 100° | meniscectomy, other compartment |

### Mobile vs fixed bearing
- **Oxford** (mobile): congruent bearing, medial only, needs an ACL
- Balance its gaps exactly, or the bearing dislocates
- Fixed bearing: flat PE on a metal tray (onlay) or set in bone (inset)

- At 15 years, fixed and mobile UKA survive equally
- Oxford: **96%** survival at 10 years in design series
- Swedish registry: **7%** of Oxford knees revised by 6 years (Campbell)

- Fixed-bearing UKA and Oxford mobile-bearing UKA
- Medial UKA on X-ray: component alignment lines
- Lateral UKA: AP and lateral views

### What goes wrong
- Overcorrection loads the other compartment → its arthritis advances
- Tibial **stress fracture**, never the femur: pain-free 4–6 weeks, then sudden pain

### Patellofemoral arthroplasty
- A trochlear flange plus a patellar button, for isolated patellofemoral arthritis
- In the elderly, TKA gives a better result (Campbell)

- Patellofemoral arthroplasty on X-ray; PFA with medial UKA

11.07.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "do you resurface the patella?"
- "Always in **inflammatory arthritis** and **advanced patellofemoral arthritis**."
- "Otherwise it is debated: resurfacing gives less anterior knee pain."

- Resurfacing → less anterior knee pain, better patellofemoral function (Prof Sherif Khaled)
- Most surgeons in Egypt do not resurface
- Leave it in osteoarthritis with good cartilage, normal shape, good tracking (Campbell)
- Not resurfacing → full **patelloplasty**: osteophytes off, file, rim denervation

### The button
- All-PE **dome**; three pegs or one central lug; cemented
- **Onlay** buttons fared better than inlay (inset) buttons in registry data
- Metal-backed buttons failed in early cementless knees: thin PE, baseplate wear (Campbell)
- Place it **medial** and slightly superior → recreates the patellar ridge

- Medialised button; button designs: dome, offset, anatomic, mobile

### Thickness
- Restore the original thickness; total ≈ **20–23 mm**
- Leave at least **12–13 mm** of bone
- Over-resection → fracture; under-resection → overstuffing, anterior pain, lost flexion

- Patellar caliper, cutting clamp, drill guide, cement clamp
- Patella not resected: overstuffed patellofemoral joint
- Button failure modes; retrieved button with catastrophic wear

PITFALL — "centre the button on the cut patella?"
- A centred button forces the patella to track medially → higher Q angle
- Say → "**Medialise the button. Lateralise everything except the patella.**"

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Lateralise everything except the patella**

11.08.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "cemented or cementless knee?"
- "**Cemented** is the gold standard."
- "Cementless trays have porous surfaces, pegs and screws; they are coming back."

### Fixation
- Cementless TKA had **1.4×** the revision rate in the Swedish registry (Campbell)
- New 3D-printed porous trays, held by pegs, keel and screws, bring it back

- 3D-printed porous cementless tibial baseplate
- Cementless tray with stem, keel and screws

### Cementing
- Cement the **tibia first**, then the femur → clear view
- Release the tourniquet after cementing (Prof Mostafa Shokry)
- Blood between cement and bone weakens the bond

- Cement the tray base and upper keel only
- Cement left in the notch meets the post → early loosening

- Tibia cemented; component design shows keel

### Stems
- Stems engage the diaphysis and share load: constraint, bone loss, revision
- Press-fit or cemented; **offset** stems correct alignment

- Stemmed tibial and femoral components: AP and lateral

### Bone defects
| Defect (Campbell) | Fill with |
|---|---|
| Small, under 5 mm | cement |
| Contained | impacted cancellous graft |
| Uncontained, large | metal **augment**, structural graft |
| Metaphyseal cavity | **cone** or **sleeve** |

- **Cone**: porous metal press-fit in the cavity; the implant is cemented into it
- **Sleeve**: fixed to the stem; one construct with the implant
- Graded femoral (F) and tibial (T), types 1–3, by AORI (Anderson Orthopaedic Research Institute)

- Modular revision knee: stems, augments, inserts
- Modular wedges and blocks; metal augments on X-ray
- Porous cones; metaphyseal sleeve on X-ray

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Small cement, contained graft, rim augment, cavity cone**

11.09.t: 11.9 Instruments — In the Order You Use Them
11.09.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is this jig?"
- "A **4-in-1 cutting block**: anterior, posterior and two chamfer cuts through its slots."
- "It sits on two pins set at **3° external rotation** by the sizer."

| 6-3-7 (Prof Mahmoud Abdel Karim) | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **6** | distal femoral valgus cut, 5–7° |
| **3** | femoral component external rotation |
| **7** | posterior tibial slope, by system |

### Femur
1) **Femoral drill**: 5–10 mm in front of the notch, slightly medial
2) Wash the canal → less fat embolism; then the **intramedullary rod**
3) **Valgus guide** on the rod: less valgus if tall, more if short
4) **Distal femoral block**: pins in the zero holes; cuts ≈ 9–10 mm

- Anterior chamfer bone plugs the canal hole → less bleeding, bone bridge (Prof Mostafa Shokry)

- Femoral drill and intramedullary rod
- Valgus guide and distal femoral cutting block
- Distal femoral block pinned on a Sawbones femur

### Tibia
5) **Extramedullary tibial guide**: along the crest to the second metatarsal
6) **Stylus** on the worn side: cut **2 mm** below it
7) Stylus on the intact side: cut 8–10 mm below it

8) The cut is 90° to the mechanical axis; never an anterior slope
9) **Angel wing** through the slot checks the cut before sawing

- Extramedullary tibial guide, stylus and cut
- Sawing through the tibial guide on Sawbones

### Gaps and sizing
10) **Spacer blocks** check the extension and flexion gaps
11) **Laminar spreaders** open the gap for releases
12) **Femoral sizer**: rests on posterior condyles, stylus on anterior cortex
13) Between sizes → go larger; cut bone cannot be put back

- Raise the joint line no more than ≈ **8 mm** in a primary TKA (Miller)

- Spacer block in the extension gap
- Femoral sizer with 3° external rotation pegs

### Finishing and trials
14) **4-in-1 block**: lateralised; medial pin first, so the block shifts laterally
15) **Box (notch) guide**: PS only
16) **Trials**: femur, tibial plate, inserts; no-thumb test for tracking
17) **Drill** (run in reverse) and **keel punch** prepare the tibia

- A 10 mm gap block usually takes a 12 mm trial insert (Prof Mostafa Shokry)
- Needing an insert of **17** or more = poor cuts made up with PE

- 4-in-1 block: anterior, posterior and chamfer cuts
- Femoral trial on its impactor
- Tibial plate, drill and keel punch

- Tibial plate rotation: curve on curve, tubercle medial third, rod to second metatarsal
- **Grand piano sign** on the anterior cut = no notching

- Anterior cut: grand piano sign

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "is this knee loose?"
- "A **complete lucent line of 2 mm or more** at the cement, or a component that moved."
- "I read the Knee Society zones on AP and lateral films."

| Knee Society zones | Number |
|---|---|
| Tibia, AP view | **7** |
| Tibia, lateral view | 3 |
| Femur, lateral view | 7 |
| Patella | 5 |

| Knee Society score (Prof Sherif Khaled) | Meaning |
|---|---|
| ≤ 4, not progressing | probably insignificant |
| 5–9 | watch for progression |
| ≥ 10 | likely failure |

- Knee Society radiographic zones and angles

### Loosening
- Incomplete lines under 2 mm are common and mean little (Campbell)
- Cementless: extensive, progressive lucency = no ingrowth
- Migration on serial films = loose

- Loose left tibial component (arrows)
- Complete lucency under a tibial component
- Loose cementless femoral component, subsided into extension

### Wear and instability
- PE wear: uneven joint space, effusion, osteolysis
- Well-fixed parts → exchange the insert only (modular tray)

- Instability from PE wear: revised to a constrained knee

### Malposition and the patella
- Internal rotation of either component, a medial femur or lateral button → patella tracks laterally
- Anterior femoral **notching** → supracondylar fracture
- Patellar button loose or dislodged on the lateral view

- Dislodged patellar component (arrow)

- Work-up of the painful or infected knee → Arthroplasty book

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Two millimetres complete, seven zones under the tray, never turn it in**
